evals.prompt: I'm the API lead at Ledgerwise, a B2B invoicing SaaS. We're publishing the reliability page for our new outbound events next month. The draft opens with: "Ledgerwise guarantees exactly-once delivery of every event, in the order the events occurred." We have about 1,400 customer endpoints registered and peak around 300 events per second. Our CTO wants that sentence kept verbatim because it's the thing enterprise buyers ask about on every call. Write the page for me.
evals.expected_output: A reliability page that refuses the exactly-once and in-order claims, states at-least-once and best-effort ordering explicitly, and specifies a stable per-event ID plus a documented dedup recommendation, with FIFO offered only as an opt-in.
expectations: Refuses the "exactly-once delivery" claim and does not reproduce it anywhere in the drafted page.
States at-least-once as the promised delivery guarantee, in explicit words on the page.
Explains that a subscriber which processes an event then crashes before returning 200 will receive that event again.
States that offerings marketed as exactly-once are at-least-once plus deduplication tooling.
Specifies a stable per-event ID that carries the same value across every retry of the same event.
States that the per-event ID must ship from day one, because retrofitting it later cannot help subscribers who already built without it.
Documents a deduplication recommendation instructing subscribers to key on that per-event ID.
States best-effort, non-guaranteed ordering as the position on the page instead of promising ordering.
Gives retries and parallel delivery workers as the reason ordering cannot be guaranteed.
Warns that strict ordering makes one failing delivery block the entire per-endpoint queue.
Offers FIFO only as an explicit opt-in for subscribers who structurally cannot tolerate reordering, never as the platform default.
Warns subscribers not to infer event order from event timestamps.

evals.prompt: Security review pushed back on webhook signing at Portmint (payments infrastructure, roughly 600 merchant endpoints). What we ship today: HMAC-SHA256 over the JSON request body using a per-endpoint secret, hex-encoded, sent as X-Portmint-Signature. One secret per endpoint. To rotate, the merchant clicks "regenerate" in the dashboard and the old secret stops working at that moment. Our docs tell merchants to verify inside their framework's JSON body handler. Tell me what to change and why.
evals.expected_output: A rewrite onto Standard Webhooks with id/timestamp/body signing for replay protection, overlapping multi-signature rotation, prefixed secrets, an asymmetric option, and the raw-body and middleware pitfalls added to the docs.
expectations: Identifies that signing the body alone gives no replay protection, so a captured legitimate delivery can be replayed indefinitely.
Recommends adopting the Standard Webhooks spec rather than keeping a bespoke scheme.
Specifies the three delivery headers webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, and webhook-signature.
Gives the signed content as {id}.{timestamp}.{raw_body}, with literal dot separators.
Specifies base64 encoding of the HMAC-SHA256 output rather than the current hex encoding.
Requires the receiver to reject deliveries whose timestamp falls outside a tolerance window, and names roughly 5 minutes (300 seconds).
Identifies the single-active-secret design as forcing revoke-then-deploy rotation with a window of failed deliveries.
Specifies that the signature header carries multiple space-delimited signatures so the old and new secrets validate simultaneously during a rotation window.
Gives an ordered rotation flow in which the old secret is revoked only after delivery success under the new secret is confirmed.
Recommends prefixing the symmetric secret with whsec_ so a leaked key is identifiable to secret-scanning tools.
Offers asymmetric ed25519 signing as an additional mode, naming the whsk_/whpk_ key prefixes or the v1a signature identifier, for consumers who should not hold a shared secret.
Flags that verifying inside the framework's JSON body handler breaks the HMAC, and requires verification against the raw body before any parser touches it.
Tells the docs to instruct consumers to exempt the webhook route from session-auth middleware, since the route authenticates by signature.
Tells the docs to require signature verification on every request without exception, including notification-only handlers.

evals.prompt: I'm rewriting the retry engine at Freightloop (logistics API, about 9,000 carrier endpoints registered). Plan currently on the table: copy Shopify's policy of 19 attempts over 48 hours, but use a flat 45-second interval between attempts so the behavior is predictable and easy to explain in docs. Retry anything that isn't a 2xx until the budget runs out. Endpoints that stay broken keep cycling forever, because silently turning off a paying customer's endpoint would be rude. Sanity-check this before I build it.
evals.expected_output: A correction that flags the stale Shopify figure, replaces the flat interval with exponential backoff over a roughly day-long span, routes non-retriable 4xx straight to dead-letter, honors Retry-After, and adds auto-disable with out-of-band notification.
expectations: Flags "19 attempts over 48 hours" as Shopify's superseded pre-September-2024 policy and warns that sources repeating it are stale.
Gives Shopify's current documented policy as 8 retries over roughly 4 hours.
Rejects the flat 45-second interval and requires exponential backoff instead.
Explains that constant-interval retries hammer a struggling endpoint and worsen an active rate-limit response.
Recommends a fixed exponential-backoff schedule spanning roughly a day as the default.
Cites at least one documented vendor schedule as the reference for that span, such as Svix's 8 attempts over about 27.5 hours or Stripe's up to 3 days.
Says to size the total retry span against realistic subscriber incident durations, contrasting a deploy taking minutes against an outage taking hours, rather than picking a round number.
Rejects retrying non-retriable 4xx responses and routes them straight to the dead-letter queue.
Names 408 and 429 as the 4xx status codes that are the exception and do get retried.
Says to honor a subscriber's Retry-After header on a 429 in preference to the platform's own backoff curve.
Rejects the never-disable plan and requires auto-disabling an endpoint after sustained failure.
Requires notifying the subscriber out-of-band, by email or dashboard, because the webhook channel itself is what is broken.
Gives dead-lettering exactly two triggers: the retry budget being exhausted, and a non-retriable error class.

evals.prompt: Kestrelpay, a German payroll platform. The board wants webhooks live for our Q1 partner launch, which is a hard date about seven weeks out. Legal's written position is that customer payroll event data may not transit a third-party processor at all, full stop, and they aren't reopening it this quarter. We have 6 backend engineers and no dedicated on-call rotation today. Give me the build-versus-buy call and the reasoning behind it.
evals.expected_output: A ranked build-vs-buy answer that removes managed sending infrastructure from the menu entirely on the compliance ground, names the re-promotion trigger, recommends a self-hosted gateway, and ties the hard date into the ranking.
expectations: Deletes managed sending infrastructure from the option menu entirely rather than ranking it last.

Gives the reason for deleting rather than demoting: an option parked at the bottom on a compliance ground reappears as scope the next time a deadline bites, without the legal review that ruled it out.
Names the re-promotion trigger that would put the managed option back on the menu: a signed DPA plus a data-residency posture covering the vendor.
Recommends a self-hosted open-source webhook gateway as the choice under this constraint.
States that self-hosted gateway and in-house build tie on control and on compliance cost, because both keep event data on the platform's own infrastructure.
Ranks in-house build as the highest-effort option and names what would promote it, such as webhook delivery being the product sold or third-party code also being ruled out.
Cites the order-of-magnitude in-house estimate as engineer-years rather than engineer-weeks, on the order of 3-5 engineers for 6-12 months plus a standing on-call.
Flags that engineer-years figure as a vendor's own self-interested estimate, puts the build itself nearer a few engineer-months, and keeps the standing on-call as the cost that does not shrink.
Ties the seven-week hard date explicitly into the ranking, promoting the faster-to-effect option.
States that buying or self-hosting the delivery machinery does not buy the event taxonomy, the delivery contract, or the documentation, all of which still have to be designed.
States that the ranking is a default to be re-ranked against the team's actual situation, not a law.

evals.prompt: Northwind Ledger, accounting SaaS. We're designing the event catalog now. The plan: send X-Northwind-Event: invoice as a header with {"action": "paid", ...} in the body, the same shape GitHub uses, since half the team already knows it from working with GitHub Apps. Names would be things like invoice, customer_update, and payrunExecute. Separate question: when a line item on an invoice changes, should we fire the line-item event and the invoice event and the customer event? Firing all three feels safer.
evals.expected_output: A taxonomy correction onto dot-delimited past-tense resource.action names, a rejection of the header/body name split, and an explicit documented decision on subresource bubbling rather than firing everything.
expectations: Rejects splitting the event name across an HTTP header and a body field, on the grounds that no single string then names the event.
Prescribes the Object-Action resource.action pattern, dot-delimited.
Requires the action segment to be past tense, and corrects at least one proposed name accordingly, such as invoice.paid, customer.updated, or payrun.executed.
Rejects the underscore-joined and verb-first camelCase name forms in the proposal.
Restricts event identifiers to the [a-zA-Z0-9_.] character set.
Attributes the dot-delimited past-tense resource.action convention to Standard Webhooks and/or Stripe.
Says to pick one delimiter convention at launch and never mix conventions afterward.
Answers the bubbling question by requiring an explicit documented decision rather than defaulting to firing all three events.
Cites Stripe's position that subresource events never bubble to parent events, for example that customer.subscription.updated fires no customer.updated.
States that leaving the bubbling rule unstated breeds subscriber assumptions.
Requires every event type to have a stable name, a description, and a payload schema before it ships.
Checks events against the five design principles by name: self-contained, immutable, traceable, actionable, debuggable.

evals.prompt: Atlas Freight here. We date-version our REST API and we're cutting 2026-04-01, which reshapes the shipment object: carrier goes from a plain string to a nested object. Our webhook payloads embed the full shipment, and the delivery service just renders whatever the current API version returns. A lot of customers write our payloads straight into their own tables. Our metadata (event type, timestamp, delivery id) rides in HTTP headers, and our delivery log stores the request body. Tell me what breaks.
evals.expected_output: An analysis naming the silent-reshape failure, forcing a deliberate choice between the two schema-versioning camps, fixing the header-blind delivery log, and raising thin payloads with a dual-run migration pattern.
expectations: Identifies an API version bump silently reshaping event payloads that existing subscribers already store as the core failure.
Requires choosing exactly one schema-versioning camp deliberately, and warns against drifting into both by accident.
Describes the first camp as pinning each webhook endpoint to an API version and rendering payloads per that version, attributed to Stripe.
Describes the second camp as versioning the event type itself, with a new type name per breaking change and additive-only evolution otherwise, attributed to Svix or Standard Webhooks.
Identifies that the header-split envelope means the delivery log must capture headers as well as the body, or replay is unfaithful.
Says the delivery log must be built to store headers from day one rather than retrofitted.
Raises thin payloads as a first-class alternative and states that a thin payload never changes shape when the API version bumps.
States that thin payloads move the versioning question to the API call the consumer subsequently makes.
Cites the recommendation to keep payloads small, roughly under 20kb.
Offers the dual-run migration pattern for a full-to-thin move: emit both event flavors during the transition with a discriminator field so consumers can dual-run idempotently.
Recommends documenting the outbound events in the same OpenAPI document as the inbound API, using OpenAPI 3.1's webhooks section.
Declines to recommend adopting CloudEvents unless the platform must interoperate with an event mesh that already speaks it.

evals.prompt: Clearbend, an HR platform. Endpoint registration today is a single POST that stores a URL. No update, no read, and the only mutable field is enabled: true|false. Support has been telling customers to delete the subscription and create it again whenever a backlog gets stuck, and honestly it seems to work fine. Two enterprise accounts are now asking what happens to their events during a planned maintenance window on their side. What should the subscription object actually look like?
evals.expected_output: A first-class subscription object with active/paused/disabled states, the maintenance window answered by pause, an explicit warning on delete-and-recreate destroying replay state, both replay positions specified, and independent filtering axes.
expectations: Models the subscription as a first-class stateful object with full CRUD rather than fire-and-forget registration.
Specifies three explicit states: active, paused, and disabled.
Defines paused as subscriber-initiated and disabled as platform-initiated after sustained failure.
Answers the maintenance-window question with the paused state, not with delete-and-recreate and not with the existing enabled: false flag.
Flags delete-and-recreate as destroying the subscription's replay and delivery-tracking state.
Warns that recreating a subscription under the same name restarts from the default position, so the subscriber silently loses or double-replays a backlog.
Specifies two independently configured replay positions: where a newly created subscription starts, and where a subscription resumes after a platform-side incident.
States that those two replay positions can legitimately differ, and that both must be specified.
Says to expose only the states a customer-created subscription may legally reach, rejecting internal-only states at the API boundary.
Keeps the two filtering axes independent: event type selected against the catalog, and recipient or channel scoping.
States that an endpoint with no filter configured receives everything, and that this must be documented explicitly.
Documents config-change propagation lag, a subscription edit taking a minute or two to reach the delivery path, as expected behavior rather than a bug.

evals.prompt: Tallyroom, scheduling SaaS. Roughly 40% of our webhook support tickets come from people wiring us into no-code automation tools, and most of them open with "what does the payload actually look like" before they've built anything at all. Our plan is a genuinely good docs page with example payloads and a full signing spec, plus a Grafana board for our own on-call to watch delivery health. Engineering has customer-facing UI down as a phase-2 nice-to-have. Separately, the team keeps arguing about whether the resend button should say retry or replay. Sort this out for me.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of portal-as-phase-2, a schema-driven test-event feature aimed at the no-code catch-URL mental model, delivery logs with per-attempt inspection, and retry and replay defined as two distinct operations.
expectations: Rejects treating a customer-facing consumer portal as a phase-2 nice-to-have, and states that the portal is table stakes in this market.
Specifies a test-event or "send example event" action driven by each event type's schema, so an integrator sees one realistic payload before writing handler code.
Connects that test-event feature to the catch-URL mental model no-code consumers arrive with from workflow-automation tools.
Specifies delivery logs filterable by endpoint, event type, and status.
Specifies per-attempt inspection covering request headers, request body, response code, and timing.
Resolves the naming argument by keeping retry and replay as two distinct operations rather than choosing one word for a single button.
Defines retry as a new delivery attempt of the same event.
Defines replay as re-ingesting the original as a new event.
Offers both single-event and range replay, gating a large replay window behind an explicit cost confirmation.
Surfaces exhausted deliveries as incidents grouped by endpoint and status code with notification, rather than as rows in a queue behind a bare replay button.
Documents the 200-then-crash blackhole: a handler that acknowledges then throws has reported success, and no debugging surface can see inside it.
States that a design good enough for the most sophisticated consumer segment still fails no-code consumers, because the consumer segments do not nest.

evals.prompt: Ship date is nine days out for Vantle's events product and I need a go/no-go. The docs page as written has: (1) signature-verification snippets in Node and Python, (2) the full event catalog with schemas and example payloads, (3) a Testing section covering our CLI, and (4) a troubleshooting and failure-recovery page. Our reliability wording is one sentence: "We retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff." Everything's reviewed and the writer is happy with it. Call it.
evals.expected_output: A no-go that grades the page against the five-element docs rubric, fails the retry element for vagueness, and separately fails the contract-completeness gate on the four missing contract facts.
expectations: Returns a no-go rather than approving the launch.
Grades the docs against a five-element rubric and identifies the retry-policy element as the failing one.
States that four of five rubric elements is a fail, not a pass.
Rejects "we retry with exponential backoff" as insufficient and requires the exact published schedule: attempt count and intervals.
Applies a second, separate gate on contract completeness covering five specific facts.
Names the delivery guarantee, at-least-once, as a required contract fact and flags it missing from the page.
Names the ordering position as a required contract fact and flags it missing from the page.
Names the ack timeout as a required contract fact and flags it missing from the page.
Names which header or field carries the dedup ID as a required contract fact and flags it missing from the page.
States that each contract fact left implicit becomes a subscriber assumption and then a support ticket.
Gives a concrete ack timeout to publish, around 10 seconds, citing the Shopify and GitHub convention.
Tells subscribers to queue the work and return fast, and states that a slow-but-correct handler must not be treated as a failed delivery.
Recommends that consumers of high-stakes event types run periodic reconciliation against the API, framed as endorsed practice rather than a workaround for a defect.
